A1.justification: Both PDFs describe VersaPRM and retain the same core pipeline, datasets, and principal experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original PRM training and evaluation results, reranking and search experiments, training ablations, and a manual audit of synthetic labels.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds held-out-domain evaluations, further ablations, open-ended questions, error examples, and iterative-refinement results.

M1.justification: The final VersaPRM architecture, loss, initialization, and fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. v2 adds experimental procedural extensions: meaning-preserving rewrite augmentation, self-filtered retraining, and one-step refinement using PRM scores as feedback (Appendices B.2–B.3 and G.2). These supplement the existing method without replacing its central pipeline.

E1.justification: The original training sources and 14-domain MMLU-Pro coverage are retained. Appendix G.1 adds a limited but distinct task: answering 116 existing law questions with their answer choices removed. This extends evaluation beyond multiple choice, while the held-out-domain experiments change training splits within existing domain coverage.

E2.justification: The main math-PRM comparator suite is retained. Appendix B.5 newly evaluates Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct directly as a step judge, with reported comparisons in Figures 16–17. Those comparisons also include new self-filtered, rewrite-augmented, and prompt-ablated VersaPRM variants.

E3.justification: v2 enlarges the manual label audit from 30 to 64 questions and specifies a 30-question subset for the simplified-prompt audit. New evaluation designs include five domain-holdout controls, open-ended law questions graded by Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and one-step refinement evaluated by average Pass@1 over 1,754 questions. The established main benchmark protocol remains intact.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's counterfactual, training-configuration, and aggregation analyses, v2 adds domain-holdout tests, rewrite augmentation, self-filtering, an end-to-end labeling-prompt ablation, manually analyzed successes and failures, and iterative refinement. These investigate transfer, supervision quality, robustness, and failure conditions. Counterfactual augmentation is retained and incorporated into expanded comparisons, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals for manual annotation agreement: 0.69–0.89 for CoTs labeled correct and 0.63–0.79 for those labeled incorrect. v1 reported point estimates alone. This is a localized addition to uncertainty reporting, concerning label quality rather than repeated training runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain their numerical results, but v2 adds extensive holdout, augmentation, judge-baseline, open-ended, failure-case, and DeepSeek-R1 Philosophy results. The enlarged audit reports 80%/71% agreement instead of 83%/70% on the smaller sample. The new refinement experiment reports Pass@1 of 51% without refinement, 45% with VersaPRM, and 44% with Qwen-2.5-Math-PRM.

T1.justification: The PRM definition, aggregation formulas, and inference equations in Section 3 are retained. Beam-search and MCTS pseudocode match across v1 Appendix B and v2 Appendix C. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, five introduction contributions, and central conclusion retain the same claims: math PRMs generalize poorly beyond mathematics, and synthetic multi-domain supervision produces a broadly effective VersaPRM with released data, code, and models. The additions principally support and qualify these existing headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 interprets held-out-domain performance as evidence beyond broader training coverage and acknowledges some benefit from learning the question format. Appendix F adds explanations of factual, arithmetic, and answer-consistency failures; Appendix G.2 proposes score-induced bias as an explanation for unsuccessful refinement. Section 7 also raises possible preference for Llama-family generators, substantially expanding applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 supplies prompts and operational details for rewriting, ablated labeling, open-ended generation and grading, and refinement, plus the 0.4 self-filtering threshold. It newly discloses AWS Bedrock batch inference and generation/labeling cost below $100. Original training hyperparameters and access information remain unchanged. Reproducibility is locally limited by Figure 15 listing a ground-truth answer despite describing its omission.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning through CoT's domain-dependent benefits, compute-optimal training, teacher–student distillation, and Constitutional AI, adding works by Sprague, Hoffmann, Hinton, Gu, Bai, and others. New appendices also connect filtering and refinement to relevant prior research. The original math-PRM literature remains represented.

P1.justification: The main seven-section narrative and much existing prose remain intact. Revisions concentrate on related work, the DeepSeek discussion, future directions, and explanatory passages. Existing counterfactual material is regrouped into Appendix B, and an appendix roadmap is added; much remaining appendix movement is renumbering rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds held-out-domain plots, a Philosophy panel to the DeepSeek figure, expanded ablation grids, open-ended results, prompt displays, and highlighted error examples. Most existing plots are retained. Figure 2 removes the ground-truth input box despite its continued use in the text, and Figure 17's legend says Best of N although its caption identifies WMV.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central generalization claim through held-out-domain controls and comparison with the 70B labeler used directly as a judge. The larger audit with confidence intervals, downstream labeling ablation, and candid failure and negative-refinement results also improve assessment of reliability and applicability. Open-ended evidence remains preliminary and LLM-graded, and new prompt/legend inconsistencies are drawbacks, but these localized issues do not outweigh the substantial gains in experimental support.
